claim: Neural network function is based upon the patterns and types of connections made between neurons.
source: Neural network function is based upon the patterns and types of connections made between neurons.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural networks presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this manuscript.

claim: Neuronal synapses come in two types: chemical and electrical.
source: Neuronal synapses are adhesions specialized for communication and they come in two types, chemical and electrical.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about synapse types.

claim: Communication at chemical synapses occurs via neurotransmitter release.
source: Communication at chemical synapses occurs via neurotransmitter release whereas electrical synapses utilize gap junctions for direct ionic and metabolic coupling.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about chemical synapse function.

claim: Electrical synapses utilize gap junctions for direct ionic and metabolic coupling.
source: Communication at chemical synapses occurs via neurotransmitter release whereas electrical synapses utilize gap junctions for direct ionic and metabolic coupling.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about electrical synapse function.

claim: Electrical synapses are often viewed as symmetrical structures, with the same components making both sides of the gap junction.
source: Electrical synapses are often viewed as symmetrical structures, with the same components making both sides of the gap junction.
evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the field prior to this study.

claim: A broad set of electrical synapses in zebrafish require two gap-junction-forming Connexins for formation and function.
source: By contrast, we show that a broad set of electrical synapses in zebrafish, Danio rerio, require two gap-junction-forming Connexins for formation and function.
evidence: This is supported by genetic and immunohistochemical data showing loss of synapses in mutants for both connexins.

claim: One Connexin functions presynaptically while the other functions postsynaptically in forming the channels at zebrafish electrical synapses.
source: We find that one Connexin functions presynaptically while the other functions postsynaptically in forming the channels.
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments showing differential requirements for each connexin.

claim: Electrical synapses in the Mauthner circuit are required for the speed and coordination of escape responses.
source: We also show that these synapses are required for the speed and coordination of escape responses.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral analysis showing delayed and uncoordinated escape responses in connexin mutants.

claim: Chemical synapses are broadly used within the nervous system and are overtly asymmetric at the molecular and functional level.
source: Chemical synapses are broadly used within the nervous system and are overtly asymmetric at the molecular and functional level, with communication between neurons achieved via presynaptic neurotransmitter release and postsynaptic neurotransmitter reception.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about chemical synapse organization.

claim: Electrical synapses are found throughout the brain from inception to adulthood and contribute to function from sensation to central processing to motor output.
source: Electrical synapses are best known for their roles in early nervous system development, however they are found throughout the brain from inception to adulthood and contribute to function from sensation to central processing to motor output (Hormuzdi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Electrical synapses are generally viewed as molecularly and functionally symmetric, allowing for very fast bidirectional ionic and metabolic neuronal communication.
source: Electrical synapses are generally viewed as molecularly and functionally symmetric, allowing for very fast bidirectional ionic and metabolic neuronal communication (Connors and Long, 2004).
evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Neuronal gap junctions are formed from plaques of tens to thousands of channels between neurons.
source: This direct route of communication is achieved by neuronal gap junctions (GJs) that are formed from plaques of tens to thousands of channels between the neurons (Raviola and Gilula, 1973; Hormuzdi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Unique GJ-forming proteins can be contributed asymmetrically from each side of the synapse in invertebrates.
source: While often viewed as simple channels, work in invertebrates has found that unique GJ-forming proteins can be contributed asymmetrically from each side of the synapse (Phelan et al., 2008; Starich et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on invertebrate electrical synapses.

claim: Molecular asymmetry can create functional asymmetry (rectification) in ionic flow through gap junctions in invertebrates.
source: Moreover, the molecular asymmetry can create functional asymmetry (rectification) in ionic flow through the GJ (Phelan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Electron microscopy and electrophysiology suggests that electrical synapse structure and function can be asymmetric in vertebrate nervous systems.
source: In vertebrate nervous systems electron microscopy and electrophysiology suggests that electrical synapse structure and function can also be asymmetric (Brightman and Reese, 1969; Rash et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The genetic basis for molecular asymmetry at vertebrate electrical synapses has never been identified prior to this study.
source: However, the genetic basis for such molecular asymmetry at vertebrate electrical synapses has never been identified.
evidence: This represents a gap in knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: Neuronal gap junction channels are composed of two hemi-channels, one contributed by each neuron, that interact via their extracellular domains.
source: Each channel is composed of two hemi-channels, one contributed by each neuron, that interact via their extracellular domains to form the channel (Figure 1A) (Connors and Long, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gap junction structure, supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Vertebrate GJ-forming proteins are the Connexins while invertebrates use an evolutionarily distinct but functionally equivalent set of Innexins.
source: Vertebrate GJ-forming proteins are the Connexins (Cx) while invertebrates use an evolutionarily distinct but functionally equivalent set of Innexins (Phelan, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In mammals there are 21 genes encoding Cx proteins of which five are known to be expressed in neurons and to form electrical synapses.
source: In mammals there are 21 genes encoding Cx proteins of which five are known to be expressed in neurons and to form electrical synapses (Connors and Long, 2004; Söhl et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A partial genome duplication that occurred in teleost fish has increased the number of Cx-encoding genes.
source: A partial genome duplication that occurred in teleost fish has increased the number of Cx-encoding genes, and the ensuing evolutionary trajectories saw some genes being duplicated and others lost (Eastman et al., 2006; Cruciani and Mikalsen, 2007; Zoidl et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on teleost genome evolution.

claim: Heterotypic GJs between cells in non-neuronal tissue are common in vertebrates.
source: In vertebrates, heterotypic GJs between cells in non-neuronal tissue are common (Goodenough and Paul, 2009), however it has been notoriously difficult to identify heterotypic Cx configurations at electrical synapses in neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: It has been notoriously difficult to identify heterotypic Cx configurations at electrical synapses in neurons.
source: In vertebrates, heterotypic GJs between cells in non-neuronal tissue are common (Goodenough and Paul, 2009), however it has been notoriously difficult to identify heterotypic Cx configurations at electrical synapses in neurons.
evidence: This represents a challenge in the field that this study addresses.

claim: The Mauthner circuit coordinates an escape response to a variety of threatening stimuli.
source: The Mauthner circuit coordinates an escape response to a variety of threatening stimuli and produces the fastest sensorimotor reflex performed by fish (~5 milliseconds (ms) to initiate, ~10 ms to complete) (Eaton et al., 1977; Fetcho, 1991; Burgess and Granato, 2007; Satou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on Mauthner circuit function.

claim: The Mauthner circuit produces the fastest sensorimotor reflex performed by fish (~5 milliseconds to initiate, ~10 ms to complete).
source: The Mauthner circuit coordinates an escape response to a variety of threatening stimuli and produces the fastest sensorimotor reflex performed by fish (~5 milliseconds (ms) to initiate, ~10 ms to complete) (Eaton et al., 1977; Fetcho, 1991; Burgess and Granato, 2007; Satou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The Mauthner circuit is a combination of electrical, excitatory chemical, and inhibitory chemical synapses.
source: The Mauthner circuit that produces the escape is a combination of electrical, excitatory chemical, and inhibitory chemical synapses contained within a relatively simple set of neurons that must be coordinated to ensure fast and robust escapes (Fetcho, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Auditory afferents make prominent and stereotyped mixed electrical and glutamatergic chemical synapses at Club Ending synapses onto Mauthner neurons.
source: To do so, vibrational stimuli are transmitted to the Mauthner neurons via the VIIIth cranial nerve auditory afferents, which make prominent and stereotyped mixed electrical and glutamatergic chemical synapses at so-called Club Ending synapses, hereafter called the Aud/M synapse (Pereda et al., 2004; Yao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mauthner sends a contralateral projection down the length of the spinal cord where it activates primary motorneurons in each hemisegment.
source: Mauthner in turn sends a contralateral projection down the length of the spinal cord where it activates primary motorneurons (MNs) in each hemisegment and drives the stereotypical C-bend-shaped escape away from stimulus (Fetcho, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The projecting Mauthner axon activates CoLo interneurons in each segment via excitatory electrical synapses.
source: The projecting Mauthner axon concurrently activates CoLo interneurons in each segment via excitatory electrical synapses; CoLo in turn re-crosses the spinal cord and inhibits MNs on the stimulus side, thereby ensuring coordinated turns away from the stimulus (Satou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CoLo interneurons re-cross the spinal cord and inhibit motor neurons on the stimulus side, ensuring coordinated turns away from the stimulus.
source: The projecting Mauthner axon concurrently activates CoLo interneurons in each segment via excitatory electrical synapses; CoLo in turn re-crosses the spinal cord and inhibits MNs on the stimulus side, thereby ensuring coordinated turns away from the stimulus (Satou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The disconnect3 (dis3) mutation causes a complete loss of Cx36 staining at the M/CoLo synapses.
source: We identified a mutation we called disconnect3 (dis3) that caused a complete loss of Cx36 staining at the M/CoLo synapses (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cx36 staining was disrupted at Mauthner electrical synapses and other electrical synapses in dis3 mutants across all timepoints examined (2 to 14 dpf).
source: Cx36 staining was disrupted at Mauthner electrical synapses and other electrical synapses in dis3 mutants across all timepoints examined (2 to 14 dpf).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data across developmental timepoints.

claim: The stereotyped number of Mauthner and CoLo neurons was not disrupted in dis3 mutants.
source: The stereotyped number of Mauthner and CoLo neurons was not disrupted in dis3 mutants: Mauthner –wildtype, heterozygous, and mutant animals had 2 ± 0 Mauthners / animal; CoLo – wildtype, heterozygous, and mutant avg. 1.975 ± 0.06, 2 ± 0.06, and 2 ± 0 CoLos/8 segments / animal, respectively (segments 5–12 were counted, mean ± standard deviation, n = 5, 11, 5 for wildtype, heterozygous, and mutant, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative cell counting data.

claim: In dis3 mutants the M and CoLo neurites contact one another in the spinal cord similar to wildtype.
source: Moreover, in dis3 mutants the M and CoLo neurites contact one another in the spinal cord similar to wildtype (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The gene disrupted by the dis3 mutation may have a specific role in electrical synapse formation.
source: These results suggest that the gene disrupted by the dis3 mutation may have a specific role in electrical synapse formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that neuron number and contact are normal but synapses are lost.

claim: RNA-seq-based mapping identified an ~1.8 megabase region of homozygosity on chromosome 5 in dis3 mutants.
source: The sequences were aligned to the genome and single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were identified in the wildtype pool to serve as mapping markers. The SNP frequency was assessed in the mutant pool, identifying an ~1.8 megabase (Mb) region of homozygosity on chromosome 5 in dis3 mutants (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq mapping data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Two missense changes were found in the gjd1a/cx34.1 gene in dis3 mutants.
source: Within this region we used the RNA-seq data to look for potentially deleterious mutations and found that there were two missense changes to a Cx-encoding gene (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: gjd1a/cx34.1 is highly related to the mammalian gjd2 gene encoding Cx36.
source: This gene is highly related to the mammalian gjd2 gene encoding Cx36 (see below).
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison and phylogenetic analysis presented later in the manuscript.

claim: Larvae homozygous for the gjd1afh436 frameshift mutation phenocopy the loss of Cx36-staining at M/CoLo synapses observed in the dis3 mutants.
source: We found that larvae homozygous for the frameshift mutation (gjd1afh436/fh436) phenocopy the loss of Cx36-staining at M/CoLo synapses observed in the dis3 mutants; moreover, gjd1afh436 failed to complement the dis3 mutation (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1G and complementation testing.

claim: gjd1a/cx34.1 is required for M/CoLo electrical synapse formation.
source: We renamed the dis3 mutation gjd1afh360 and conclude that gjd1a/cx34.1 is required for M/CoLo electrical synapse formation.
evidence: This is supported by genetic complementation and phenocopy data.

claim: All four zebrafish Cx36-related proteins share greater than 85% amino acid identity to each other and to mammalian Cx36 proteins.
source: Within this group of four Cx-encoding genes, all of the predicted proteins share greater than 85% amino acid identity to each other and to mammalian Cx36 proteins (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by amino acid alignment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The main variation in protein sequence among the four Cx36-related proteins arises in the intracellular loop, with some modest variation in the C-terminal tail.
source: The main variation in protein sequence arises in the intracellular loop, with some modest variation in the C-terminal tail (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by amino acid alignment and schematic shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The four zebrafish Cx36-related proteins represent two distinct Cx sub-families.
source: We examined the evolutionary relationship between these proteins and found that they represent two distinct Cx sub-families (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In basal vertebrates (lamprey) there is only one gene within the Cx36-related family.
source: In basal vertebrates (lamprey) we found only one gene within the family, this gene was subsequently duplicated creating two sub-families – the Cx35/36 proteins encoded by gjd2 genes and the Cx34 proteins encoded by genes we have named gjd1.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Genes within both the gjd1 and gjd2 families are found in lineages up to and including birds, but in mammals the gjd1 family has apparently been lost.
source: Genes within both of these families are found in lineages up to and including birds, but in mammals the gjd1 family has apparently been lost.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In bony fishes, including zebrafish, the gjd1 and gjd2 gene families underwent another duplication event, resulting in the four extant genes.
source: In bony fishes, including zebrafish, these gene families underwent another duplication event (Postlethwait et al., 2004), resulting in the four extant genes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2C and citation to previous literature.

claim: The gjd1b/cx34.7 and gjd2b/cx35.1 genes are expressed in the nervous system of zebrafish.
source: Previous work has found that the gjd1b/cx34.7 and gjd2b/cx35.1 genes are expressed in the nervous system of zebrafish, analogous to gjd2 (Cx36) expression in mammals (Li et al., 2009; Carlisle and Ribera, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: All four of the gjd1 and gjd2 genes in zebrafish are enriched for nervous system expression while being reduced or absent from other tissues.
source: We examined published RNA-seq and EST datasets (Ensembl: WTSI stranded RNA-Seq, WTSI, KIT, Yale [Yates et al., 2016] and the UCSC Genome Browser [Kent et al., 2002]) and found that all four of the gjd1 and gjd2 genes in zebrafish are enriched for nervous system expression while being reduced or absent from other tissues.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published RNA-seq and EST datasets.

claim: All of the gjd1/2 genes have the potential to play broad roles in neural circuit formation and function.
source: Together it appears that all of the gjd1/2 genes have the potential to play broad roles in neural circuit formation and function.
evidence: This is inferred from the nervous system-enriched expression pattern of all four genes.

claim: gjd1a/cx34.1 mutants lose not only the M/CoLo synapses in the spinal cord, but also the Aud/M synapses, as well as other electrical synapses made onto the Mauthner cell body.
source: We found that gjd1a/cx34.1 mutants affected not only the M/CoLo synapses in the spinal cord, but also the Aud/M synapses, as well as other electrical synapses made onto the Mauthner cell body (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants lose Mauthner electrical synapses in the hindbrain and spinal cord.
source: In analyzing mutants for the other three genes, we found that gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants also lost Mauthner electrical synapses in the hindbrain and spinal cord (Figure 3G–I)
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: gjd1b/cx34.7 and gjd2b/cx35.1 mutants have no effect on Cx36 staining at Mauthner synapses.
source: while gjd1b/cx34.7 and gjd2b/cx35.1 had no effect on Cx36 staining (Figure 3J,K).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3J,K.

claim: In gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants there was a complete absence of detectable Cx protein at synapses throughout the Mauthner circuit.
source: In quantifying the amount of Cx36-staining at Mauthner synapses we found that in gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants there was a complete absence of detectable Cx protein at synapses throughout the Mauthner circuit.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data.

claim: In gjd1a/cx34.1 mutants the Cx36 staining at M/CoLo synapses was lost, but approximately 30% of staining remained at the Aud/M synapses.
source: In gjd1a/cx34.1 mutants the Cx36 staining at M/CoLo synapses was lost, but we note that ~ 30% of staining remained (an ~4 fold reduction) at the Aud/M synapses (Figure 3E,J,K).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3E,J,K.

claim: The residual Cx36 staining at Aud/M synapses in gjd1a/cx34.1 mutants was not eliminated in double or triple mutants between gjd1a/cx34.1 and gjd1b/cx34.7 or gjd2b/cx35.1.
source: This residual staining was not eliminated in double or triple mutants between gjd1a/cx34.1 and gjd1b/cx34.7 or gjd2b/cx35.1 (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: The gap junctions that form the Mauthner circuit electrical synapses require both gjd1a/cx34.1 and gjd2a/cx35.5 for their formation.
source: On the whole we conclude that the gap junctions that form the Mauthner circuit electrical synapses require both gjd1a/cx34.1 and gjd2a/cx35.5 for their formation.
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis showing loss of synapses in mutants for both genes.

claim: In both gjd1a/cx34.1 and gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants no neurobiotin was transferred from Mauthner to CoLo.
source: In both gjd1a/cx34.1 and gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants we found that no Nb was transferred from Mauthner to CoLo (Figure 4C–G).
evidence: This is supported by neurobiotin dye transfer experiments shown in Figure 4C-G.

claim: In gjd1b/cx34.7 and gjd2b/cx35.1 mutants neurobiotin transfers from Mauthner to CoLo similar to wildtype.
source: By contrast, we found that in gjd1b/cx34.7 and gjd1b/cx35.1 mutants Nb transfers from Mauthner to CoLo similar to wildtype (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by neurobiotin dye transfer experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Mauthner circuit electrical synapses are dependent on both Cx34.1 and Cx35.5 proteins for their function.
source: That Nb passage is completely blocked in both gjd1a/cx34.1 and gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants supports the idea that Mauthner circuit electrical synapses are dependent on both Cx34.1 and Cx35.5 proteins for their function.
evidence: This is supported by neurobiotin dye transfer experiments.

claim: There is an intimate interaction between Cx34.1 and Cx35.5 required for the establishment of Mauthner electrical synapses.
source: Taken together these data suggest that there is an intimate interaction between these two Cxs required for the establishment of M electrical synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutual requirement of both connexins for synapse formation and function.

claim: Cx34.1 and Cx35.5 staining overlapped nearly completely throughout the hindbrain and spinal cord.
source: Cx34.1 and Cx35.5 staining overlapped nearly completely throughout the hindbrain and spinal cord, but there were rare examples where staining was apparent for only one of the two Cx proteins (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by dual immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At Mauthner circuit electrical synapses Cx34.1 and Cx35.5 staining was completely overlapping at the individually identifiable Aud/M and M/CoLo synapses.
source: At Mauthner circuit electrical synapses Cx34.1 and Cx35.5 staining was completely overlapping at the individually identifiable Aud/M and M/CoLo synapses in the hindbrain and the spinal cord (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by dual immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: In gjd1a/cx34.1 mutants Cx34.1 staining was lost.
source: In gjd1a/cx34.1 mutants we found that Cx34.1 staining was lost while in the gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants we found that Cx35.5 staining was lost supporting both the specificity of the antibodies as well as the deleterious nature of the mutations (Figure 5D–I).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D-I.

claim: In gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants Cx35.5 staining was lost.
source: In gjd1a/cx34.1 mutants we found that Cx34.1 staining was lost while in the gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants we found that Cx35.5 staining was lost supporting both the specificity of the antibodies as well as the deleterious nature of the mutations (Figure 5D–I).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D-I.

claim: In gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants Cx34.1 staining was lost from Aud/M and M/CoLo synapses.
source: In gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants we found that Cx34.1 staining was lost from Aud/M and M/CoLo synapses suggesting Cx34.1 requires Cx35.5 for its localization at Mauthner synapses (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5G-I.

claim: Cx34.1 requires Cx35.5 for its localization at Mauthner synapses.
source: In gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants we found that Cx34.1 staining was lost from Aud/M and M/CoLo synapses suggesting Cx34.1 requires Cx35.5 for its localization at Mauthner synapses (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing loss of Cx34.1 in gjd2a mutants.

claim: In gjd1a/cx34.1 mutants Cx35.5 was completely lost from M/CoLo synapses.
source: In gjd1a/cx34.1 mutants we found that Cx35.5 was completely lost from M/CoLo synapses (Figure 5F)
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In gjd1a/cx34.1 mutants residual Cx35.5 staining was found at Aud/M synapses similar to what was observed with the human Cx36 antibody.
source: and residual Cx35.5 staining was found at Aud/M synapses similar to what was observed with the human Cx36 antibody (Figure 5D,E; Figure 3D,E,J,K).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D,E and Figure 3D,E,J,K.

claim: Both Cx34.1 and Cx35.5 are broadly expressed and used throughout the hindbrain and spinal cord of zebrafish.
source: Altogether our results suggest that both Cx34.1 and Cx35.5 are broadly expressed and used throughout the hindbrain and spinal cord of zebrafish.
evidence: This is supported by widespread colocalization of both proteins shown in immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Where Cx34.1 and Cx35.5 colocalize their mutual presence supports the robust localization of the other at electrical synapses.
source: Moreover, while each Cx can apparently be used independently, where Cx34.1 and Cx35.5 colocalize their mutual presence supports the robust localization of the other at electrical synapses.
evidence: This is supported by the loss of one connexin when the other is mutated.

claim: When presynaptic neurons (auditory afferent neurons in the hindbrain or Mauthner in the spinal cord) lacked gjd1a/cx34.1 the electrical synapses were normal.
source: Similarly, when presynaptic neurons (auditory afferent neurons in the hindbrain [Figure 6F] or Mauthner in the spinal cord [Figure 6I]) lacked gjd1a/cx34.1 the electrical synapses were normal.
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments shown in Figure 6F,I.

claim: When the postsynaptic neuron (Mauthner in the hindbrain or CoLo in the spinal cord) lacked gjd1a/cx34.1 the electrical synapses were affected.
source: However, when the postsynaptic neuron (Mauthner in the hindbrain [Figure 6G,H] or CoLo in the spinal cord [Figure 6J]) lacked gjd1a/cx34.1 the electrical synapses were affected.
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments shown in Figure 6G,H,J.

claim: Removing gjd2a/cx35.5 function presynaptically, but not postsynaptically, resulted in the loss of associated electrical synapses.
source: Conversely, we found exactly the opposite requirement for gjd2a/cx35.5: removing its function presynaptically, but not postsynaptically, resulted in the loss of associated electrical synapses (Figure 6K–O).
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments shown in Figure 6K-O.

claim: Presynaptic removal of gjd2a/cx35.5 resulted in a complete loss of Cx36 staining at any associated synapse.
source: Moreover, presynaptic removal of gjd2a/cx35.5 resulted in a complete loss of Cx36 staining at any associated synapse, while postsynaptic loss of gjd1a/cx34.1 resulted in no staining at M/CoLo synapses and an ~4 fold reduction of Cx36 staining at Aud/M synapses (Figure 6P,Q)
evidence: This is supported by quantification of chimeric transplantation experiments shown in Figure 6P,Q.

claim: Postsynaptic loss of gjd1a/cx34.1 resulted in no staining at M/CoLo synapses and an ~4 fold reduction of Cx36 staining at Aud/M synapses.
source: Moreover, presynaptic removal of gjd2a/cx35.5 resulted in a complete loss of Cx36 staining at any associated synapse, while postsynaptic loss of gjd1a/cx34.1 resulted in no staining at M/CoLo synapses and an ~4 fold reduction of Cx36 staining at Aud/M synapses (Figure 6P,Q)
evidence: This is supported by quantification of chimeric transplantation experiments shown in Figure 6P,Q.

claim: At M/CoLo synapses Cx35.5 and Cx34.1 are the exclusive pre- and postsynaptic Cxs, respectively.
source: This suggests that at M/CoLo synapses Cx35.5 and Cx34.1 are the exclusive pre- and postsynaptic Cxs, respectively, while at the Aud/M synapses Cx35.5 is the sole presynaptic Cx while Cx34.1 is required postsynaptically for the majority of GJ channels (Figure 6P,Q).
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments showing complete loss when either is removed from the appropriate side.

claim: At the Aud/M synapses Cx35.5 is the sole presynaptic Cx while Cx34.1 is required postsynaptically for the majority of GJ channels.
source: This suggests that at M/CoLo synapses Cx35.5 and Cx34.1 are the exclusive pre- and postsynaptic Cxs, respectively, while at the Aud/M synapses Cx35.5 is the sole presynaptic Cx while Cx34.1 is required postsynaptically for the majority of GJ channels (Figure 6P,Q).
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments showing partial rescue when gjd1a is removed postsynaptically.

claim: Within the single Mauthner neuron both Cx-encoding genes are required for electrical synapse formation, but their functions are spatially restricted to the dendrite (gjd1a/cx34.1) versus the axon (gjd2a/cx35.5).
source: We note that even within the single Mauthner neuron both Cx-encoding genes are required for electrical synapse formation, but their functions are spatially restricted to the dendrite (gjd1a/cx34.1, Figure 6G,H) versus the axon (gjd2a/cx35.5, Figure 6N).
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments showing differential requirements in different compartments of the same neuron.

claim: gjd2a/cx35.5 and gjd1a/cx34.1 are required pre- and postsynaptically, respectively, at Mauthner circuit electrical synapses.
source: We conclude that gjd2a/cx35.5 and gjd1a/cx34.1 are required pre- and postsynaptically, respectively, at Mauthner circuit electrical synapses.
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments.

claim: Some GJ channels at Mauthner electrical synapses are heterotypic, with unique Cxs used on each side of the synapse.
source: The above transplant experiments suggest that some GJ channels at Mauthner electrical synapses are heterotypic, with unique Cxs used on each side of the synapse.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential pre- and postsynaptic requirements for different connexins.

claim: A trans-synaptic interaction between the Cxs is required for stabilization, and thereby detection via antibody staining, at the Mauthner synapses.
source: Moreover, our results suggest that a trans-synaptic interaction between the Cxs is required for stabilization, and thereby detection via antibody staining, at the Mauthner synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of one connexin when the other is mutated.

claim: When the postsynaptic neuron was wildtype in a gjd1a/cx34.1 mutant host the electrical synapses were rescued.
source: We found that when the postsynaptic neuron was wildtype in a gjd1a/cx34.1 mutant host the electrical synapses were rescued (Figure 7A,B,D); however, when the presynaptic neuron was wildtype there was no rescue (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments shown in Figure 7A,B,D.

claim: When the presynaptic neuron was wildtype in a gjd1a/cx34.1 mutant host there was no rescue of electrical synapses.
source: We found that when the postsynaptic neuron was wildtype in a gjd1a/cx34.1 mutant host the electrical synapses were rescued (Figure 7A,B,D); however, when the presynaptic neuron was wildtype there was no rescue (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: A wildtype presynaptic neuron was sufficient to rescue the synapse in a gjd2a/cx35.5 mutant.
source: Conversely, a wildtype presynaptic neuron was sufficient to rescue the synapse in a gjd2a/cx35.5 mutant (Figure 7G), but had no effect when the wildtype neuron was postsynaptic (Figure 7E,F,H).
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments shown in Figure 7G.

claim: A wildtype postsynaptic neuron had no effect on rescuing synapses in a gjd2a/cx35.5 mutant.
source: Conversely, a wildtype presynaptic neuron was sufficient to rescue the synapse in a gjd2a/cx35.5 mutant (Figure 7G), but had no effect when the wildtype neuron was postsynaptic (Figure 7E,F,H).
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments shown in Figure 7E,F,H.

claim: Cx35.5 is sufficient to rescue the synapse if it is present in the presynaptic neurons.
source: In other words, Cx35.5 is sufficient to rescue the synapse if it is present in the presynaptic neurons while Cx34.1 is sufficient to rescue the synapse if it is present in the postsynaptic neuron.
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments showing rescue with wildtype presynaptic neurons in gjd2a mutants.

claim: Cx34.1 is sufficient to rescue the synapse if it is present in the postsynaptic neuron.
source: In other words, Cx35.5 is sufficient to rescue the synapse if it is present in the presynaptic neurons while Cx34.1 is sufficient to rescue the synapse if it is present in the postsynaptic neuron.
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments showing rescue with wildtype postsynaptic neurons in gjd1a mutants.

claim: Electrical synapse formation in the Mauthner circuit requires presynaptic Cx35.5 and postsynaptic Cx34.1.
source: Altogether we conclude that electrical synapse formation in the Mauthner circuit requires presynaptic Cx35.5 and postsynaptic Cx34.1 and that robust Cx localization at the synapse requires a trans-synaptic interaction with an appropriate Cx in an adjacent cell.
evidence: This is supported by chimeric transplantation experiments showing differential requirements.

claim: Robust Cx localization at the synapse requires a trans-synaptic interaction with an appropriate Cx in an adjacent cell.
source: Altogether we conclude that electrical synapse formation in the Mauthner circuit requires presynaptic Cx35.5 and postsynaptic Cx34.1 and that robust Cx localization at the synapse requires a trans-synaptic interaction with an appropriate Cx in an adjacent cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutual requirement and rescue experiments.

claim: At 6 dpf there are approximately six auditory afferent neurons making mixed electrical/glutamatergic chemical synapses onto Mauthner.
source: At 6 dpf there are approximately six auditory afferent neurons making mixed electrical/glutamatergic chemical synapses onto Mauthner (Aud/M); the electrical component of the postsynaptic response occurs 1–3 ms after afferent stimulation and happens just prior to that of its glutamatergic counterpart (Yao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The electrical component of the postsynaptic response at Aud/M synapses occurs 1–3 ms after afferent stimulation and happens just prior to that of its glutamatergic counterpart.
source: At 6 dpf there are approximately six auditory afferent neurons making mixed electrical/glutamatergic chemical synapses onto Mauthner (Aud/M); the electrical component of the postsynaptic response occurs 1–3 ms after afferent stimulation and happens just prior to that of its glutamatergic counterpart (Yao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Electrophysiology at the M/CoLo synapse suggests a single, excitatory electrical coupling allowing Mauthner to activate CoLo during an escape.
source: By contrast, electrophysiology at the M/CoLo synapse suggests a single, excitatory electrical coupling allowing Mauthner to activate CoLo during an escape (Satou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Electrical synapses have unique effects on the initiation (Aud/M) and coordination (M/CoLo) of the Mauthner-induced escape response.
source: Thus, electrical synapses are suggested to have unique effects on the initiation (Aud/M) and coordination (M/CoLo) of the Mauthner-induced escape response.
evidence: This is inferred from the known circuit organization and electrophysiology.

claim: gjd1a/cx34.1 and gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants produced SLCs at similar frequencies compared to their wildtype siblings.
source: We found that mutants produced SLCs at similar frequencies compared to their wildtype siblings (Figure 8A, note that we found no difference between wildtype siblings from the gjd1a/cx34.1+/− or gjd2a/cx35.5+/− crosses and so have collapsed these two groups into a single wt data point in Figure 8; individual statistics can be found in the source data and lead to the same conclusions).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Both gjd1a/cx34.1 and gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants initiated escape responses ~2 ms (40%) slower than their wildtype siblings.
source: However, we found that both gjd1a/cx34.1 and gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants initiated escape responses ~2 ms (40%) slower than their wildtype siblings (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A subset of escape responses in cx mutants (~20% in each genotype) occurred with an abnormally shallow maximum angle of the C-bend as well as abnormally slow maximum angular velocities.
source: However, a subset of mutant responses (~20% in each genotype) occurred with an abnormally shallow maximum angle of the C-bend (Figure 8C, arrow) as well as abnormally slow maximum angular velocities (Figure 8D, arrow).
evidence: This is supported by kinematic analysis shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: Both gjd1a/cx34.1 and gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants produced abnormal postural responses to the auditory startle stimuli.
source: These abnormal responses suggested a defect in performing the stereotyped C-bend shape of the escape response and so we reanalyzed the video data from these events and found that both gjd1a/cx34.1 and gjd2a/cx35.5 mutants produced abnormal postural responses to the auditory startle stimuli (Figure 8I–L).
evidence: This is supported by video analysis shown in Figure 8I-L.

claim: Electrical synapses contribute to the speed and coordination of the Mauthner induced escape response.
source: From these data we conclude that electrical synapses contribute to the speed and coordination of the Mauthner induced escape response.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral analysis showing delayed and uncoordinated responses in connexin mutants.

claim: Differences in the pre- and postsynaptic Cxs could bias the passage of ionic flow through the GJ creating a rectified electrical connection.
source: One intriguing possibility is that differences in the pre- and postsynaptic Cxs would bias the passage of ionic flow through the GJ creating a rectified electrical connection (Palacios-Prado et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is speculation based on known properties of heterotypic channels, supported by citation.

claim: In Drosophila, Shaking-B(Neural +16) and Shaking-B(lethal) form a molecularly asymmetric synapse that allows for biased current flow when paired in apposing Xenopus oocytes.
source: Indeed such is the case for two Innexins, Shaking-B(Neural +16) and Shaking-B(lethal), that in Drosophila form a molecularly asymmetric synapse; when these hemi-channels are paired in apposing Xenopus oocytes they allow for biased current flow (Phelan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In adult goldfish freeze-fracture immunolabeling and electron microscopy suggest that the Aud/M (club ending) synapses of Mauthner are molecularly asymmetric.
source: In adult goldfish freeze-fracture immunolabeling and electron microscopy (EM) suggest that the Aud/M (club ending) synapses of Mauthner are molecularly asymmetric (see below for discussion of Cx usage) and electrophysiology found that ionic flow was preferentially directed from the post- to presynaptic terminal; the authors suggested that this functional asymmetry leads to cooperativity amongst the multiple converging auditory afferent axons thereby promoting the Mauthner escape response (Rash et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In adult goldfish Aud/M synapses, ionic flow was preferentially directed from the post- to presynaptic terminal.
source: In adult goldfish freeze-fracture immunolabeling and electron microscopy (EM) suggest that the Aud/M (club ending) synapses of Mauthner are molecularly asymmetric (see below for discussion of Cx usage) and electrophysiology found that ionic flow was preferentially directed from the post- to presynaptic terminal; the authors suggested that this functional asymmetry leads to cooperativity amongst the multiple converging auditory afferent axons thereby promoting the Mauthner escape response (Rash et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The molecular asymmetry of Cxs suggests that GJ-associated proteins may also be asymmetrically distributed.
source: The molecular asymmetry of Cxs we identify suggests that GJ-associated proteins may also be asymmetrically distributed.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding of molecular asymmetry in connexins.

claim: The autism associated gene neurobeachin was required postsynaptically for electrical synaptogenesis.
source: Intriguingly, we previously found that the autism associated gene neurobeachin, which encodes a scaffolding protein thought to act within the trans-Golgi network, was required postsynaptically for electrical synaptogenesis (Miller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Previous freeze fracture immuno-EM work in goldfish suggested that Cx35.1 and Cx34.7 may create the Aud/M synapses.
source: Previous freeze fracture immuno-EM work in goldfish has instead suggested that Cx35.1 and Cx34.7 may create the Aud/M synapses, yet we find that the genes encoding these two Cxs are not required in zebrafish (Figures 3 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and comparison to current findings.

claim: Antibodies generated against Cx34.7 and Cx35.1 used in goldfish studies label zebrafish Aud/M and M/CoLo electrical synapses at larval stages from 3 to 7 dpf.
source: Second, as others have shown (Satou et al., 2009; Yao et al., 2014), we found that antibodies generated against Cx34.7 and Cx35.1 and used in the goldfish studies (Rash et al., 2013) label zebrafish Aud/M and M/CoLo electrical synapses at larval stages from 3 to 7 dpf (see Materials and methods for antibody details).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data and citation to previous work.

claim: The Cx34.7 antibody cross reacts with Cx34.1, while the Cx35.1 antibody cross reacts with Cx35.5.
source: Given the amino acid similarity of the two gjd1 proteins and the two gjd2 proteins (Figure 2), the most parsimonious scenario would be that the Cx34.7 antibody cross reacts with Cx34.1, while the Cx35.1 antibody cross reacts with Cx35.5.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic evidence and amino acid similarity.

claim: While Cx35.5 appears to be the sole presynaptic Cx at Aud/M synapses, Cx34.1 may not act alone on the postsynaptic side of the synapse.
source: We also find that while Cx35.5 appears to be the sole presynaptic Cx at Aud/M synapses (Figure 6K), Cx34.1 may not act alone on the postsynaptic side of the synapse (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is inferred from the residual staining observed when gjd1a is removed postsynaptically.

claim: Molecular asymmetries at electrical synapses are found broadly throughout the nervous systems of C. elegans, medicinal leech, D. melanogaster, and crab.
source: Molecular asymmetries at electrical synapses are not confined to fish, but are found broadly throughout the nervous systems of C. elegans (Starich et al., 2009), medicinal leech (Kandarian et al., 2012), D. melanogaster (Curtin et al., 1999; Phelan et al., 2008), crab (Shruti et al., 2014), and there have been suggestions, though no definitive proof, that such may occur in mammals as well (Cha et al., 2012; Haas et al., 2011; Zolnik and Connors, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: There have been suggestions, though no definitive proof, that molecular asymmetries at electrical synapses may occur in mammals.
source: Molecular asymmetries at electrical synapses are not confined to fish, but are found broadly throughout the nervous systems of C. elegans (Starich et al., 2009), medicinal leech (Kandarian et al., 2012), D. melanogaster (Curtin et al., 1999; Phelan et al., 2008), crab (Shruti et al., 2014), and there have been suggestions, though no definitive proof, that such may occur in mammals as well (Cha et al., 2012; Haas et al., 2011; Zolnik and Connors, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mammals appear to have lost the gjd1/cx34 family of genes, leaving only the single, related gjd2/cx36 gene.
source: If such does occur in mammalian systems it would have to rely on a different set of Cxs than in zebrafish as mammals appear to have lost the gjd1/cx34 family of genes, leaving only the single, related gjd2/cx36 gene (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: There are four other Cxs known to make electrical synapses in mammals.
source: However, there are four other Cxs known to make electrical synapses in mammals (Connors and Long, 2004; Söhl et al., 2005; Pereda, 2014), and the extent of their use and the configurations of GJs they create is poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Molecularly asymmetric electrical synapses are likely to be a part of all nervous systems.
source: We expect that molecularly asymmetric electrical synapses are likely to be a part of all nervous systems given that they underlie important functional effects on the properties of neural circuit computation (Phelan et al., 2008; Rash et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation based on widespread occurrence across species and functional importance, supported by citation.

claim: The reduction in response speed in cx mutants is likely due to the loss of the electrical component of the Aud/M synapses.
source: We prefer the model that the reduction in response speed is due to the loss of the electrical component of the Aud/M synapses (Figure 9B) given that these synapses are required for Mauthner activation and sufficient to create the fast escape response (O'Malley et al., 1996; Tabor et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from circuit organization and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings of Aud/M synapses in wildtype larval zebrafish show the electrical response occurs ~2 milliseconds faster than that of the chemical synaptic response.
source: This idea is supported by electrophysiological recordings of Aud/M synapses in wildtype larval zebrafish at stages similar to those we analyzed where the electrical response occurs ~2 milliseconds faster than that of the chemical synaptic response (Yao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The coordination defects observed in cx mutants are likely due to the loss of the M/CoLo synapses in the spinal cord.
source: We also observed that a subset of escape responses in cx mutants display coordination defects. This is likely due to the loss of the M/CoLo synapses in the spinal cord as similar behavioral defects have been observed when CoLos are laser ablated or when strychnine is used to block inhibitory synapses (Satou et al., 2009; Marsden and Granato, 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from similarity to previous ablation and pharmacological experiments, supported by citation.

claim: Loss of gjd2/cx36 in mice results in defects in vision.
source: Indeed, loss of gjd2/cx36 in mice results in defects in an ever increasing list of neurological functions including vision (Güldenagel et al., 2001; Cowan et al., 2016), smell (Christie et al., 2005), thalamic function (Zolnik and Connors, 2016), estrous cyclicity (Campbell et al., 2011), short-term spatial memory (Allen et al., 2011), motor performance (Frisch et al., 2005), as well as others.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Loss of gjd2/cx36 in mice results in defects in smell.
source: Indeed, loss of gjd2/cx36 in mice results in defects in an ever increasing list of neurological functions including vision (Güldenagel et al., 2001; Cowan et al., 2016), smell (Christie et al., 2005), thalamic function (Zolnik and Connors, 2016), estrous cyclicity (Campbell et al., 2011), short-term spatial memory (Allen et al., 2011), motor performance (Frisch et al., 2005), as well as others.
